name: C#
description: Value vs reference types, async/await, LINQ, disposal and the .NET runtime behaviours behind them.

modules.name: Types, Memory & Disposal
modules.description: Structs, classes, boxing, nullable reference types and deterministic cleanup.

cards.answer: Structs are value types copied on assignment; classes are reference types where the reference is copied.

left.title: struct (value type)
points: Copied on assignment and when passed
Usually on the stack or inline in its owner
Great for small, immutable, short-lived data

right.title: class (reference type)
points: Reference copied; object lives on the heap
Right for identity, inheritance, larger state

cards.explanation: Guidance: make a struct only if it is small (~16 bytes or less), logically a single value, immutable and not boxed often. Mutable structs are a classic bug source because you mutate a copy without noticing.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — Choosing between class and struct

cards.prompt: What is boxing, and where does it sneak in?
cards.answer: Boxing wraps a value type in a heap object so it can be treated as `object` or an interface. It appears in non-generic collections, `object` parameters, string interpolation of value types, and calling an interface method on a struct through the interface.
cards.explanation: Each box is an allocation plus a copy plus later GC pressure. Generics avoid it — `List<int>` stores ints inline while `ArrayList` boxes each one. Constrained generic calls (`where T : IComparable<T>`) also avoid boxing that an `IComparable` parameter would cause.

cards.prompt: The GC handles memory. Why does `IDisposable` exist?
cards.answer: Because the GC only manages memory, and only nondeterministically. Files, sockets, DB connections, locks and native handles need releasing at a known moment — that is what `Dispose`, and the `using` statement that calls it, are for.
cards.explanation: Finalizers are a last-resort safety net: they run on a separate thread at an unknown time and delay collection by a full GC cycle. Implement the dispose pattern, prefer `using var`, and use `SafeHandle` rather than writing finalizers yourself.

cards.prompt: What do nullable reference types actually change at runtime?
cards.answer: Nothing. They are compile-time annotations plus flow analysis: `string?` may be null, `string` should not be, and the compiler warns where you violate it. The runtime representation is identical.
cards.explanation: Enable with `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>`. The value is in the warnings, so treat them as errors in CI — half-enabled nullability gives false confidence. The `!` null-forgiving operator silences the compiler and should be rare and commented.

cards.answer: Value-based equality, a generated `ToString`, deconstruction, and `with` expressions for non-destructive mutation. `record struct` does the same for value types.
cards.explanation: Records suit DTOs, messages and domain values where two instances with the same data should be equal. Use `init`-only setters to make them genuinely immutable; the equality is still shallow, so a record holding a `List<T>` compares by list reference.

modules.name: Async & LINQ
modules.description: The async state machine, deadlocks, deferred execution and the traps behind both.

cards.prompt: Why can this deadlock in a UI or classic ASP.NET app?
cards.answer: `.Result` blocks the thread that owns the synchronization context; the continuation after `await` needs that same context to resume, so both wait forever. Await all the way up, or use `ConfigureAwait(false)` in library code.
cards.explanation: By default a continuation is posted back to the captured context. Blocking that context on the task creates a cycle. The rule: never block on async code — `async` should propagate to the entry point. ASP.NET Core has no such context, but libraries still cannot assume that.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — Async guidance: avoid sync over async

cards.answer: There is no Task to await or observe, so the caller cannot know when it finishes, and an exception is thrown on the synchronization context — typically crashing the process instead of surfacing as a faulted task.
cards.explanation: The single legitimate use is an event handler, whose signature demands `void`. Everywhere else return `Task` (or `ValueTask` for hot paths that usually complete synchronously) so failures and completion are observable.

LINQ query operators are deferred — `Where` builds an iterator and executes only when enumerated, at which point it sees the current contents of the list. Call `.ToList()` to snapshot, and beware enumerating an expensive query twice by accident.

cards.answer: IEnumerable runs the delegate in memory; IQueryable builds an expression tree a provider translates — typically into SQL.

left.title: IEnumerable<T>
points: Filters after data has been fetched

right.title: IQueryable<T>
points: LINQ to a provider (EF Core, etc.)
Filters translate into the WHERE clause
Unsupported expressions throw or fall back

cards.explanation: Casting an `IQueryable` to `IEnumerable` too early is a classic performance bug: the whole table is pulled into memory and filtered there. Watch for it whenever you call a custom method inside a query.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — Client vs server evaluation

cards.prompt: How should a long-running async API support being cancelled?
cards.answer: Accept a `CancellationToken` parameter, pass it to every async call you make, and check `token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` around synchronous loops.
cards.explanation: Cancellation is cooperative — nothing forcibly aborts a task. A token that is accepted but never forwarded is worse than none, because callers believe cancellation works. `CancellationTokenSource` also provides timeouts via `CancelAfter`.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — Cancellation in managed threads

cards.answer: They give a type-safe, bounds-checked view over contiguous memory — arrays, stack buffers or unmanaged memory — so you can slice and parse without allocating substrings or copies.
cards.explanation: `Span<T>` is a ref struct: stack-only, so it cannot be stored in a field or captured by an async method. `Memory<T>` is the heap-storable equivalent for async paths. Together they eliminate most parsing allocations in hot code.
